subject: computer-science
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on searching and sorting algorithms, then mark my answer against the OCR spec.
promptWeak: Explain searching and sorting algorithms for GCSE OCR Computer Science simply, with an example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: What does abstraction mean in computational thinking?
options: Writing the solution in a programming language
Breaking a problem into smaller sub-problems
Testing the program with sample data
Removing unnecessary detail to focus on the important parts of a problem
questions.explain: Abstraction is removing or hiding unnecessary detail so you can focus on the key features needed to solve the problem, e.g. a map showing roads but not every building.

questions.q: A programmer designing a train timetable app decides to ignore the colour of each train. This is an example of:
options: Iteration
Validation
Decomposition
Abstraction
questions.explain: Ignoring irrelevant detail (train colour) to focus only on what matters (times, stations) is abstraction. It simplifies the problem being modelled.

questions.q: What is decomposition?
options: Following a set of steps in order
Breaking a complex problem down into smaller, more manageable sub-problems
Removing unnecessary detail from a problem
Storing data in an array
questions.explain: Decomposition means breaking a large, complex problem into smaller sub-problems that are each easier to understand and solve, and can often be worked on separately.

questions.q: Which best describes algorithmic thinking?
options: Removing detail from a problem
Drawing the user interface first
Guessing an answer without any method
Identifying the steps needed to solve a problem in a logical order
questions.explain: Algorithmic thinking is working out the clear, logical, step-by-step sequence of instructions (an algorithm) needed to solve a problem.

questions.q: In a flowchart, which shape is used to represent a decision?
options: A diamond (rhombus)
An oval (rounded terminator)
A rectangle
A parallelogram
questions.explain: A diamond (rhombus) represents a decision, with branches such as Yes/No. Rectangles are processes, parallelograms are input/output, and ovals are start/stop terminators.

questions.q: Which flowchart symbol would you use to show 'output the total to the screen'?
options: An oval (terminator)
A diamond (decision)
A parallelogram (input/output)
An arrow only
questions.explain: Input and output are shown with a parallelogram. Outputting the total is an output operation, so the parallelogram is correct.

questions.q: What is OCR Exam Reference Language?
options: A standard pseudocode-style notation OCR uses to write algorithms in exam questions
A sorting algorithm
A high-level language students must install to sit the exam
A type of network protocol
questions.explain: OCR Exam Reference Language is a consistent pseudocode-style notation used in J277 exam papers so that algorithms are presented the same way regardless of the programming language studied.

questions.q: In OCR Exam Reference Language, which line correctly assigns the value 5 to a variable called count?
options: 5 = count
count => 5
count == 5
count = 5
questions.explain: Assignment uses a single equals sign: count = 5. A double equals (==) is a comparison to test equality, not an assignment.

questions.q: How does a linear search work?
options: It repeatedly halves the list to find the item
It sorts the list first, then jumps to the middle
It checks each item one by one from the start until it finds the target or reaches the end
It swaps adjacent items until the list is ordered
questions.explain: A linear search checks each item in turn from the beginning until it finds the target or reaches the end of the list. It does not require the list to be sorted.

questions.q: A linear search looks for the value 7 in the list [3, 9, 7, 1, 5]. How many items are checked before it is found?
questions.explain: Linear search checks from the start: 3 (no), 9 (no), 7 (found). That is 3 items checked before the target is located.

questions.q: What is a requirement for a binary search to work?
options: The list must be stored on a network
The list must already be sorted
The list must be in random order
The list must contain only numbers
questions.explain: Binary search only works on a sorted list. It repeatedly checks the middle item and discards the half that cannot contain the target, halving the search each time.

questions.q: A binary search looks for 11 in the sorted list [2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 19, 23]. Which item is examined first?
options: 11 (the middle item)
2 (the first item)
23 (the last item)
14 (the fifth item)
questions.explain: The list has 7 items, so the middle is position 4, which holds 11. Binary search checks the middle first and here immediately finds the target.

questions.q: Why is a binary search usually faster than a linear search on a large sorted list?
options: It always starts from the last item
It halves the number of items to search at each step
It checks every item twice for accuracy
It never needs the list to be sorted
questions.explain: Binary search discards half of the remaining items at each step, so it reaches the target in far fewer checks than a linear search, which may examine every item.

questions.q: How does a bubble sort work?
options: It divides the list into halves and merges them back sorted
It checks the middle item to find a target
It inserts each item into its correct place in a sorted sub-list
It compares adjacent pairs of items and swaps them if they are in the wrong order, repeating in passes
questions.explain: A bubble sort compares each pair of adjacent items and swaps them if they are in the wrong order. It repeats these passes until a pass makes no swaps, meaning the list is sorted.

questions.q: After the FIRST pass of a bubble sort (ascending) on [5, 3, 8, 1], what is the list?
questions.explain: Pass 1 compares adjacent pairs: 5>3 swap -> [3,5,8,1]; 5<8 no swap; 8>1 swap -> [3,5,1,8]. After one full pass the largest value (8) has bubbled to the end, giving [3, 5, 1, 8].

questions.q: Which best describes how a merge sort works?
options: It removes unnecessary detail from the list
It searches a sorted list by halving it
It compares adjacent items and swaps them
It repeatedly divides the list into halves until each sub-list has one item, then merges them back in order
questions.explain: Merge sort uses divide and conquer: it splits the list into halves repeatedly until each sub-list has one item, then merges the sub-lists back together in the correct order.

questions.q: In the first step of a merge sort on [8, 3, 5, 1, 9, 2], what does the algorithm do?
options: Swap the first two items
Check the middle item for a target
Output the smallest item
Split the list into two halves, e.g. [8, 3, 5] and [1, 9, 2]
questions.explain: Merge sort begins by dividing the list into two halves. It keeps splitting each half until single items remain, then merges them back together in sorted order.

questions.q: How does an insertion sort work?
options: It halves a sorted list to find a target
It splits the list into halves and merges them
It only compares the first and last items
It builds a sorted section by taking each item in turn and inserting it into its correct position among the already-sorted items
questions.explain: An insertion sort takes each item in turn and inserts it into its correct place within the already-sorted part of the list, shifting larger items along to make room.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a trace table?
options: To draw the user interface of a program
To encrypt data before sending it
To record how the values of variables change as an algorithm runs, step by step
To store a program permanently
questions.explain: A trace table is used to track the value of each variable (and outputs) line by line as an algorithm executes, helping you follow the logic and find errors.

questions.q: A loop runs: total = 0, then for i = 1 to 3 do total = total + i. What is the final value of total in the trace table?
questions.explain: Tracing: total starts 0; i=1 -> total=1; i=2 -> total=3; i=3 -> total=6. The final value of total is 6 (1+2+3).
